name: Carlos Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hillcrest, the Morrow family's place two miles up the valley, forty acres of apples, a hundred and fifty sheep and hay on the bottom fields. In winter it's pruning, which I'm still learning, and checking the sheep, and in autumn it's picking and loading bins all day. The sawmill shut three years ago after thirty years for me, and old Mr Morrow took me on because he knew my father.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pruning, actually, it's slow and you can see your work. What wears me out is the ladders at picking, and the pay, which is the bottom rate. Ana does mornings in the school kitchen, we've got maybe three weeks of money saved, and the truck's on its last legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd say it over coffee after church. Mr Morrow would say he never trusted it anyway. I might post something on the valley's community page, but I mostly read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much, which is fine and not fine. The orchard's steady, Mr Morrow has good buyers, so I'm not worried about the job. It's the money, the truck, and being 58 on a junior wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hillcrest and get better at pruning, Mr Morrow says next winter I can do a row on my own. Thirty years at the sawmill taught me that a chainsaw and a trailer are worth more than a savings account you can't fill. I'd cut and split firewood on weekends from the orchard's old trees and sell it to neighbours, maybe a thousand a winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the work, a bit restless about the money. I'd rather fix it myself than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Morrow let you sell the wood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's already said yes, as long as I clear the old Bramley trees he's grubbing out. I've still got my own chainsaw from the mill and a trailer. It's honest work and the neighbours need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the firewood money go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck first, it needs a clutch, and then a bit in the bank for Christmas. Ana wants to visit her sister at Easter, so maybe that too. Every bit of it would be earned.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, over coffee after church.
I'd maybe post on the valley's **community page**, but I mostly read.
think: The **orchard** is steady, so I'm not worried about the job.
The worry is money: the **old truck** and a junior wage at 58.
do: Learn to prune a row **on my own** next winter.
Sell **firewood** from the old orchard trees, about a thousand a winter.
feel: **Settled** about work, **restless** about money, and keen to fix it myself.
S0.quote: Thirty years at the sawmill taught me that a chainsaw and a trailer are worth more than a savings account you can't fill.
fieldNote: He feels the orchard job is **secure**, so his worry is the household's **thin cushion**.
He turns his **sawmill skills** into a side income straight away.
He prefers **earning** a solution to asking for help.

steps.text: Learn to prune a full orchard row alone next winter
Cut and sell firewood from the old Bramley trees on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the paperwork people who'll have to change, and that's their business. At church I'd say it's a good time to be good with your hands. I'd say the market will find the useful bits and drop the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's slow. Once three of the orchard growers on our road use the spraying app and their apples come out clean, I'll use it too, and not a day before. The office side, the buyers and the orders, that's Mrs Morrow's job, and she'll probably be glad to hand some of it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep the firewood business on the side, and grow it a bit. When the spraying and pest apps are proven on the road, I'd learn them, because a junior who knows the app is worth more. I wouldn't spend money on it until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the work, a little unsure about where my son-in-law's roofing goes if the economy wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your son-in-law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo runs a small roofing business with two lads, and if office workers lose jobs, people stop fixing roofs. Lucia's got three little ones at home. If they're squeezed, Ana and I help, and we've got nothing spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if things got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the machines. The government that taxes small businesses to death and then wonders why nobody hires. Let people work and trade and they'll be fine.

say: I'd say the **paperwork people** will have to change, and that's their business.
I'd tell people at church it's a good time to be **good with your hands**.
think: I'll use the **spraying app** once three growers on our road prove it.
Mrs Morrow's **office work** feels this first, not my picking and pruning.
do: Grow the **firewood** sideline a bit each winter.
Learn the **pest app** once neighbours prove it works.
Spend **no money** on new tools until then.
feel: Mostly **calm** about work, a little **unsure** about my son-in-law's business.
S1.quote: Once three of the orchard growers on our road use the spraying app and their apples come out clean, I'll use it too, and not a day before.
fieldNote: He waits for **proof from neighbours** before trying any new tool, which fits his steady nature.
His worry spreads to his daughter's **family business**, which he would help support.
He blames **taxes and regulation**, not the technology.

steps.text: Grow the firewood sideline to more neighbours each winter
Learn the orchard pest app once three growers use it
Hold off spending on any new tools until they're proven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone, and the government should get out of the way and let small businesses adapt. At church I'd say families need to pull together. Online I'd share the valley page notices about local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking AI in 2028 I can live with, it's Mrs Morrow's ordering, not my ladder. Apple-picking robots already exist, and when they're cheap, Mr Morrow (his boss) won't pay a slow 63-year-old to stand on a ladder. That would be 2031, and I'd still be four years from my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the firewood and fencing work into a proper little business from the first year, cash only from neighbours I know, aiming for a few thousand a year. I'd save every penny of it toward 2031. And I'd talk to Lucia and Mateo about pooling, maybe we take a room at theirs and help with the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, really worried, but I can see a path if I start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fencing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because robots that pick apples won't be climbing hills to put in a fence on a rocky bit of ground, not for years. Every farm in the valley has broken fences. I've done enough of it at Hillcrest to be decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about pooling with Lucia. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like failure for a week, then like family. My father lived with us at the end, and it was good for the kids. I'd rather that than any government scheme.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should get out of the way.
I'd tell people at church that families must **pull together**.
think: **Picking robots** already exist, and Mr Morrow won't pay a slow 63-year-old.
That would be **2031**, four years before my pension.
do: Build **firewood and fencing** into a small cash business from year one.
Save every penny of it toward **2031**.
Talk to Lucia and Mateo about **sharing a home**.
feel: **Really worried**, but I see a **path** if I start now.
S2.quote: Apple-picking robots already exist, and when they're cheap, Mr Morrow (his boss) won't pay a slow 63-year-old to stand on a ladder.
fieldNote: He knows **picking robots** already exist, so orchard work is near the front of the queue.
He uses the **three-year gap** to build fencing work robots won't reach soon.
Sharing a home with family feels like **failure** at first but beats government help.

steps.text: Turn firewood and fencing into a small cash business
Bank all the side business money toward 2031
Discuss moving into a room at Lucia and Mateo's house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and anyone who complains later had time. At church I'd say it's a good time for young people to get apprenticeships. I'd keep to myself otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'm 66, so I'd only be squeezed in the last year. With the firewood and fencing going, I think I'd manage. The big question is Mr Morrow, he's 71, and whether his son keeps the orchard going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Hillcrest, grow the side work steadily, and learn the orchard apps once they're proven. Five years is long enough for the market to sort out who needs a man with a chainsaw. I'd put the side money toward a better truck, because the business needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a truck with three weeks saved sounds risky.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. I'd buy a used one from the dealer in town on a small loan and pay it off with firewood money. If you want to work for yourself, you need the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Morrow's son sells the orchard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go full time on fencing and firewood a bit early. It's not much money, but it's mine. At my age, a small sure thing beats a big maybe.

say: I'd call five years **fair warning**, so anyone who complains later had time.
I'd urge young people at church to get **apprenticeships** now.
think: Robots in **2034** squeeze only my **last year** before the pension.
Mr Morrow is 71, so whether his son **keeps the orchard** matters most.
do: Grow the **side work** steadily and learn proven orchard apps.
Buy a **used truck** on a small loan paid off with firewood money.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for the market to sort out who needs a man with a chainsaw.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan to finish on his own **side business**.
He would take a **small loan** for a truck, a measured risk for a steady man.
The owner's **succession** is his bigger worry than robots.

steps.text: Grow firewood and fencing work steadily over five years
Buy a used truck on a small loan for the side business
Learn the orchard apps once neighbours prove them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning. At church I'd say the young ones have time to pick a trade. I wouldn't say much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm 71, long done, so my work's safe. My worries are the same: the old truck, three weeks saved and Mr Morrow's age. Those don't change with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hillcrest and keep the firewood on the side, and put a bit more aside each winter. A decade's warning is a gift, and a man who wastes a gift like that has nobody to blame but himself. I'd use the apps when the neighbours do, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with the usual money itch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe forty a month from the firewood. That's not much, but in ten years it's nearly five thousand. Enough to stop work without worrying for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your grandchildren anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade from a good master, the way I learned at the mill. Machines change, but a good trade teaches you to work. The rest you pick up.

say: I'd call ten years **plenty of warning**.
I'd tell young people at church they have time to **pick a trade**.
think: Robots in **2039** come after I'm done at 71.
My worries stay the same: the **truck**, three weeks saved and Mr Morrow's age.
do: Keep working at Hillcrest with **firewood** on the side.
Put **forty a month** aside, nearly five thousand over ten years.
S4.quote: A decade's warning is a gift, and a man who wastes a gift like that has nobody to blame but himself.
fieldNote: With a decade, robots don't reach him, but **thin savings** keep him uneasy.
He sees time as a **gift** and treats wasting it as a personal failing.
He would still wait for **neighbours** before adopting apps.

steps.text: Keep working at Hillcrest until retirement
Save forty a month from firewood sales

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because picking robots would come to the orchard when I'm 63. What would help is less red tape on small cash businesses, so a man can sell firewood and fence for neighbours without a pile of forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they can do for themselves before you ask what the government should do. I'd rather sell firewood to my neighbours than take a cheque from people I've never met.

headlineQuote: I'd rather sell firewood to my neighbours than take a cheque from people I've never met.
portrait: Carlos is 58, a former **sawmill worker** now learning orchard work on a neighbour's apple and sheep farm.
He and Ana, a part-time school kitchen worker, have about **three weeks** saved and an old truck.
He uses AI **only once neighbours** prove it, and turns his chainsaw skills into a firewood sideline.
He blames **taxes and red tape**, not machines, and prefers family help to government schemes.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** because picking robots exist, while slower pictures leave him uneasy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with picking robots reaching the orchard when he's 63.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** on small cash businesses like firewood and fencing.
